solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Could this make hot war explode?

definitions.text: Could this make hot war explode?

parts.words: Could this make hot war explode?
parts.note: surface reading: what might set off armed conflict between nations
setter's reading: a fit of temper is a small personal explosion, and the letters of 'hot war' can be blown apart to start the phrase

explanation.surface: A grave question about what might spark an all-out war.
explanation.walkthrough: To THROW A WOBBLY is British slang for having a tantrum; HOT WAR rearranged gives THROWA, a sly nod at the phrase's first two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Losing your temper is a personal explosion, so a tantrum is just the thing that could make a quarrel boil over.

clue.text: Some gunpowder, say, for crook

definitions.meaning: first meaning: gunpowder is a Chinese green tea rolled into pellets, so a bit of it is this
second meaning: cockney rhyming slang for thief

explanation.surface: A villain gets hold of some explosive powder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gunpowder' looks explosive but is a variety of tea; TEA LEAF is rhyming slang for thief.
explanation.definitionFit: Gunpowder tea is made of dried leaves, and in cockney rhyming slang the phrase stands for a thief.

clue.text: Conservative Party leads miss basic training here

indicators.note: to lead is to go in front, so the party word is placed ahead of the abbreviation for Conservative

parts.note: a reception is a formal party
standard abbreviation for Conservative
a miss is a girl

explanation.surface: Tory party bosses fail to attend basic training.
explanation.walkthrough: In England the RECEPTION CLASS is the first year of primary school, where children aged four or five start learning.
explanation.definitionFit: Children learn their earliest school skills, such as letters and numbers, in this first year of primary education.

clue.text: Vladimir in play, say, wanting one drink

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the word for one is taken out

parts.note: Vladimir spends Beckett's Waiting for Godot waiting, so he is an example of someone who waits
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: An actor playing Vladimir needs a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Vladimir and Estragon wait throughout Waiting for Godot; remove I from WAITER to leave WATER.
explanation.definitionFit: Water is the most basic beverage there is.

clue.text: Having less bread, disappeared to eat seconds

indicators.note: to eat something is to take it inside, so the phrase for disappeared wraps around the abbreviation

parts.note: wore off means faded away
s is the abbreviation for seconds

explanation.surface: Someone's food vanished while seconds were eaten, leaving less bread.
explanation.walkthrough: Bread is slang for money; S goes inside WORE OFF after the R.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread is slang for money, and being poorer than before means being in a worse financial state.

clue.text: Black sauce is something unusual

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
sauce and lip both mean cheek or impudence

explanation.surface: A dark sauce strikes someone as an odd thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sauce' looks culinary but means cheeky talk, as does lip.
explanation.definitionFit: A blip is a brief deviation from the normal pattern, an unexpected anomaly.

clue.text: Abandoned children getting away from the Tories?

parts.note: left means abandoned or deserted
wards are children under a guardian's care

explanation.surface: Deserted youngsters escape from the Conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tories are Britain's right-wing party, so moving away from them politically is heading to the left.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving politically away from the right-wing Conservatives means travelling in the direction of the left.

clue.text: Introduce Polish grammatical feature

parts.note: to present someone is to introduce them
to perfect something is to polish or refine it

explanation.surface: Launching a feature of the Polish language's grammar.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital P on 'Polish' is just its position at the start of a word in the surface; it means refine, not from Poland.
explanation.definitionFit: The present perfect is an English verb tense, as in 'I have eaten', so it is a feature of grammar.

clue.text: Cases of jaundice? Kindly, logical doctor's needed here

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so each following word gives only its first and last letters

parts.note: first and last letters
first and last letters
first and last letters

explanation.surface: A doctor is called for a case of jaundice, kindly and logically.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cases' is a medical word in the surface but means outer letters. The kindly, logical doctor is Jekyll, not his violent alter ego Hyde.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Jekyll is the respectable physician in Stevenson's tale who turns into Mr Hyde.

clue.text: Lucky figure deprived of the first course

indicators.note: deprived of the first means the opening letter is lost

parts.note: a mascot is a figure kept for luck

explanation.surface: A lucky charm figure misses out on the starter course of a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' suggests a meal but means a racecourse; ASCOT is a famous English racecourse near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a racecourse in Berkshire, home of the Royal Ascot meeting.

clue.text: Walls of residence with effective buttress

indicators.note: the walls are the outside of a building, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters
a rule in force is effective, operative

explanation.surface: A house's walls are given a sturdy supporting buttress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buttress' reads as a noun in the building surface but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To buttress is to strengthen or support, just as to reinforce is.

clue.text: Merchant who used to be a baggage-handler?

parts.note: ex means former
a porter carries luggage

explanation.surface: A trader who once carried people's luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as EX-PORTER and it describes a former porter.
explanation.definitionFit: An exporter is a trader who sells goods abroad, a kind of merchant.

clue.text: Not going straight, like a Victorian pickpocket?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: winding, full of bends
second meaning: Dickens's orphan Oliver was taught to pick pockets by Fagin, so a whimsical adjective for resembling him

explanation.surface: A crook who won't go straight, like a Dickensian thief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not going straight' also hints at criminality; the second sense adds -Y to Oliver Twist's surname, the question mark flagging the whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something winding has many turns, and being Twist-like jokingly evokes Dickens's young pickpocket.

clue.text: Following trouble, Peter's bound to succeed

parts.note: f is the abbreviation for following
to ail is to trouble
peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: After difficulties, Peter is certain to prosper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peter' looks like a name; in criminal slang a peter is a safe, and a peterman a safecracker.
explanation.definitionFit: A fail-safe system is designed so it cannot go wrong, hence certain to work.

clue.text: Admirer pinching bottom? He rectifies errors

indicators.note: to pinch here is to grip, so the admirer word squeezes the next word inside it

parts.note: a suitor admires and woos
the bottom of a river or sea is its bed

explanation.surface: An admirer pinches someone's backside, and an error is corrected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pinching bottom' paints an unwelcome advance; bottom means bed, as in seabed.
explanation.definitionFit: A subeditor at a newspaper corrects copy, fixing mistakes before printing.

clue.text: Waste matter goes here, contained by river banks

indicators.note: banks line both sides of something, so the river name surrounds the other piece

parts.note: the Ural is a river in Russia and Kazakhstan
something contained by a box is in it

explanation.surface: Rubbish floating downstream is trapped between the river banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'River banks' looks like a single phrase, but banks is a verb meaning surrounds, applied to the river's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Urine is liquid waste, and a urinal is the fixture designed to receive it.

clue.text: Maybe a Forest defender's heard, one providing the score

indicators.note: heard means the words are taken by their spoken sound rather than spelling

parts.note: a ranger patrols and protects a forest

explanation.surface: A Nottingham Forest footballer's defending is noted, by the man who scores.
explanation.walkthrough: Forest suggests Nottingham Forest football club and score a goal; in fact a forest ranger, and a musical score.
explanation.definitionFit: An arranger adapts music for performers, writing out the score.

clue.text: Primate and bishop with rings round head

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the pair of ring shapes goes either side of the head word

parts.note: an O is ring-shaped, and two rings give two
nob is slang for head

explanation.surface: An archbishop and a bishop appear with rings round their heads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' could be a senior archbishop beside the bishop; here it is the ape.
explanation.definitionFit: The bonobo is a great ape closely related to the chimpanzee, so a primate.

clue.text: Teacher with complaint or problem after retiring

parts.note: a BEd, Bachelor of Education, is a teaching degree, so stands for a teacher
a bug is a minor illness

explanation.surface: A teacher suffering an illness or a problem after retirement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' suggests leaving work but means going to bed, where this pest bites.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedbug is an insect that bites sleepers, a nuisance once you have gone to bed.

clue.text: After ruin, Penny and Bill in temporary housing

parts.note: a financial crash ruins people
p is the abbreviation for penny
a bill is a poster or advertisement

explanation.surface: After going broke, Penny and Bill end up in temporary accommodation.
explanation.walkthrough: Penny and Bill look like a couple's names; a bill is a posted notice, an ad.
explanation.definitionFit: A crash pad is somewhere to sleep for a night or two, a short-term place to stay.

clue.text: What a Republican achieved must inspire reactionary

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so the first part is drawn inside the word for achieved

parts.note: did means accomplished
eh is a request to repeat, like what?
taken as written
standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A Republican's success should energise conservatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What a Republican achieved' reads as one phrase but splits: the first three words go inside the word for achieved.
explanation.definitionFit: A diehard stubbornly resists change, and reactionary describes someone opposed to progress.

clue.text: Gull in delta with duck

parts.note: Delta is the NATO alphabet word for D
to duck is to dodge or evade

explanation.surface: A seabird and a duck share a river delta.
explanation.walkthrough: Gull, delta and duck form a birdwatcher's scene, but gull is a verb meaning fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To gull someone is to trick or deceive them, which is what deluding means.

clue.text: Stick with dullard back from house party

parts.note: to jam is to stick fast
a bore is a dull person

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: last letter

explanation.surface: A dull guest stays on at the end of a house party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House party' looks like the definition, but house only supplies its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A jamboree is a lavish celebration or large gathering, such as a scout rally.

clue.text: Asian climber in risky venture left without energy

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the following letter is surrounded

parts.note: a bet is a gamble
standard abbreviation for left
E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A mountaineer in Asia abandons a risky expedition, exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without energy' looks like lacking E; here without means outside, so BET L goes round E.
explanation.definitionFit: Betel is a climbing vine of tropical Asia, its leaves chewed with areca nut.

clue.text: Litre in fuel knocked over — it gets blown up

indicators.note: something knocked over is turned on its end, so the letters run backwards in this down light
in places the litre abbreviation inside the fuel word

parts.note: oil is a fuel
standard abbreviation for litre

explanation.surface: A litre of spilt fuel catches fire with a bang.
explanation.walkthrough: LILO is a British brand name for an inflatable airbed, used at the beach or pool.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lilo is an air mattress that must be inflated before use.

clue.text: Page in uniform: my job is emotionally difficult

parts.note: Uniform is the NATO alphabet word for U
p is the abbreviation for page
the setter's job is setting crosswords

explanation.surface: A uniformed pageboy finds his work emotionally draining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My job' is the setter speaking: their work is SETTING the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something upsetting causes distress, making it hard to cope with emotionally.

clue.text: Dry answer about ambassador's character

indicators.note: about means around, so the first pieces enclose the ambassador's abbreviation

parts.note: TT means teetotal, abstaining from alcohol
standard abbreviation for answer
His Excellency, an ambassador's title

explanation.surface: A witty reply about an ambassador's personality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry' as teetotal and HE as His Excellency are crossword staples. 'Character' suggests personality but means a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, and a letter is a written character.

clue.text: Bats maul predator which is hard to attack

indicators.note: bats means crazy, so the letters following go wild and are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Bats savage a hunting animal that is difficult to assail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the flying animals in a nature scene; it means mad, the cue to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Armour-plated means covered in protective metal sheets, so tough to penetrate in battle.
